articles.title: GVC integration, supply chain resilience, FTAs key to boost exports, high-end manufacturing: Deloitte India - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: GVC integration, supply chain resilience, FTAs key to boost exports, high-end manufacturing: Deloitte India  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
Deloitte India underscores the critical importance of strengthening India's links with global value chains to boost exports. It suggests that building resilient supply chains and optimizing free trade agreements are key strategies. Addressing vulnerabilities like supplier reliance and forming tech partnerships is vital.
Deepening integration into global value chains (GVCs), strengthening supply chain resilience and enhancing utilisation of free trade agreements (FTAs) are key to boosting the country's exports and high-end manufacturing, according to Deloitte India.
Anil Talreja, Partner, Deloitte India, said India needs to work on further reducing logistics costs through multimodal export corridors by focusing not only on infrastructure creation but also on end-to-end supply chain efficiency.
Besides, priority should be given to lowering costs associated with port handling, transportation, warehousing, rail connectivity, container availability, and last-mile logistics.
"India's next phase of export-led manufacturing must move beyond scale and assembly towards technology, value addition and deeper integration into GVCs," Talreja said, adding that the focus should be on high-potential sectors such as electronics and semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, capital goods, defence and aerospace, speciality chemicals and clean technologies.
The recent FTAs finalised by India can be leveraged as an important enabler of this process, providing access to competitively priced intermediate inputs, technology, investment and large export markets, while creating opportunities for Indian firms to integrate into supply chains of the partner, he added.
Deloitte India stated that India should assess vulnerabilities in critical supply chains, including dependence on key inputs, supplier concentration and geopolitical risks, and reduce them through alternative suppliers, technology partnerships, domestic production and strategic reserves.
It also called for aligning free trade agreements with the country's industrial strategy to attract investment, develop manufacturing ecosystems and widen export opportunities.
Rationalise tariff structures by revisiting inverted duty structures that increase input costs and reduce export competitiveness, it said.
For MSMEs, it suggested that the government support the segment in complying with rules of origin, standards and documentation requirements to make better use of preferential tariffs under free trade agreements.
MSMEs account for about 48.58 per cent of India's total exports and 45 per cent of the country's manufacturing.
He also suggested addressing certain challenges being faced by MSMEs, such as access to affordable trade finance.
"MSMEs often face challenges in securing pre- and post-shipment credit due to limited collateral, credit history, and export track record, resulting in higher financing costs. High exposure to payment and currency risks: Long export payment cycles and fluctuating exchange rates can adversely affect cash flows, pricing competitiveness, and profitability," Talreja added.

articles.title: Top 7 Manufacturing States in India in 2026: Check Which South Indian State Leads - Trade Brains
articles.summary: Top 7 Manufacturing States in India in 2026: Check Which South Indian State Leads  Trade Brains
articles.full_text:
The manufacturing sector in India is diversifying and states are developing robust manufacturing industries in the sectors such as automobiles, electronics, chemicals, textiles, pharmaceuticals, engineering, etc. However, the growth rate differs widely from state to state. The states are ranked based on the number of registered manufacturing establishments as per the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), 2024-25.
1. Tamil Nadu
Approximately 15.4% of the manufacturing units registered in India are located in Tamil Nadu, which has the maximum number of manufacturing units in the country with 41,221 units. It has an industrial network that extends from Chennai and Sriperumbudur to Hosur, Coimbatore, Tiruppur, Ranipet and Thoothukudi with automobiles, electronics, textiles, engineering, footwear and chemicals.
The state is also gaining new investments in newer manufacturing areas. During the 2026 period, L&T had an investment of ₹18,600 crore in the data centres, electronics manufacturing and shipbuilding business, including the construction of a ₹2,500-crore electronics plant in Coimbatore. Further confirming Tamil Nadu as its EV hub, Hyundai announced it will invest over ₹26,000 crore in the state during the period 2023 to 2032.
2. Gujarat
Currently, Gujarat has 33,084 registered manufacturing units which make up approximately 12.39% of the total manufacturing units in India. These factories are concentrated in Ahmedabad, Vadodara, Surat, Rajkot, Sanand, Dahej and Jamnagar. It has market strengths in chemicals, petrochemicals and engineering, automobiles, pharmaceuticals and textiles. Tata Electronics Dholera fab is a 66.2 hectares investment of ₹91,526 crore with an expected capacity of 50,000 wafers per month and 21,000 jobs. In the meantime, Micron's Sanand facility is an investment of approximately USD 2.75 billion.
3. Maharashtra
Approximately 27,379 manufacturing establishments registered in Maharashtra accounting for 10.26% of the manufacturing GVA in India. The major manufacturing hubs consist of Pune, Mumbai-Thane, Nashik, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Nagpur, which cover the automobile, engineering, pharmaceutical, chemicals and electronics sectors.
The momentum of investments is continuing to build in 2026. The proposed Bharat-Switzerland industrial enclave in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region would be spread over 5,000 acres and would witness investments of approximately ₹1.25 lakh crore, creating approximately 1.5 lakh direct and indirect jobs.
4. Uttar Pradesh
Uttar Pradesh has approximately 25,000 registered manufacturing units, which make up approximately 9.35% of the total manufacturing units in India. Its major clusters are Noida, Greater Noida, Ghaziabad, Kanpur, Lucknow and Agra with electronics, mobile phones, leather, textiles, food processing and engineering being its key industries.
The state's electronics and semiconductors industry is booming. In 2026, 206 acres of electronics projects were established at Jewar with an investment of ₹6,750 crore. The state is also promoting a semiconductor park of 1000 acres on Yamuna Expressway.
5. Andhra Pradesh
Andhra Pradesh has approximately 16,440 registered manufacturing units, which make up approximately 6.61% of the total manufacturing units in India. The manufacturing industry is distributed across Sri City, Tirupati, Visakhapatnam, Kurnool and Kadapa with electronics, automobiles, food processing, pharmaceuticals and renewable energy being the main areas. Royal Enfield cleared a manufacturing plant with an investment of ₹2,508 crore at Tirupati and Apollo Tyres approved a ₹6,100 crore plant at Sri City. There are 28 projects worth ₹22,178 crore that were approved in recent times, which are projected to generate jobs.
6. Karnataka
Karnataka has approximately 15,640 registered manufacturing units, which make up approximately 5.86% of the total manufacturing units in India. Bengaluru, Mysuru, Tumakuru, Dharwad, Kolar and Mangaluru are the key centres. It has a strong strength in electronics, automobiles, aerospace, engineering, biotechnology and machinery.
Karnataka has recently approved projects worth ₹29,679 crore which will create 66,360 jobs, in which Mahindra Aerostructures has been approved for ₹2,300 crore while Toyota Kirloskar has been approved for ₹1,200 crore. Foxconn's Devanahalli plant is an investment of ₹20,000 crore spread over 300 acres with employment in sight of 50,000 jobs. 
7. Telangana
Telangana has approximately 11,070 registered manufacturing units, which make up approximately 4.15% of the total manufacturing units in India. The leading industrial centers of the state are Hyderabad, Medchal, Sangareddy and Rangareddy, and Telangana has significant manufacturing in the pharmaceuticals, electronics, aerospace, chemicals and electrical equipment sectors.
Rashmi Group has plans for a steel plant that will generate approximately 12,000 jobs and will cost around ₹12,500 crore. Schneider Electric is also putting an investment of ₹623 crore in growing its manufacturing units at Gagillapur and Shamshabad. TCS subsidiary, HyperVault, acquired 264 acres in Hyderabad for a proposed 1GW AI data-centre facility.
Where is manufacturing employment concentrated?
Industrial jobs are also present in large numbers in the formal sector in India, especially in manufacturing. The new ASI data indicates that it is a few big industrial states that have the heaviest concentration of employment, depending on the size of their factory ecosystem.
The top 5 states in terms of manufacturing jobs in 2024-25 were Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and Haryana with over 56% of the total employment. Tamil Nadu is one of the largest employment-generating employment markets in the country, with the presence of the large Automobile, Electronics, Textile and Engineering industries.
Conclusion
India's manufacturing potential is distributed across a wide range of industrial States, with each one having its sectoral strength. In some cases, some factories are more numerous than others, in other cases, some factories are more performing in manufacturing value, employment or in investments in high-tech. These hubs are poised to become more important for India's industrial development due to new projects in sectors such as semiconductors, electronics, EVs and advanced manufacturing.

Saudi-backed Yemeni army says 700 Houthis killed in 24 hours
The Houthis’ claims that the Iran-allied armed group has targeted Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh are “misleading”, according to the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki’s remarks came on Saturday after the Houthis claimed ballistic missile and drone attacks on an Aramco oil facility near Riyadh.
The group said the assault caused large fires as fighting between the Houthis and government forces intensifies in Yemen.
In remarks carried by Saudi media Asharq Al-Awsat late on Saturday, al-Maliki claimed that the Houthis are “attempting to divert attention from the scale of the losses and the growing public anger against them”.
‘Chaos and devastation’
The development comes after the Yemeni forces “executed 257 precision targeting operations” against Houthi sites, movements, and military capabilities on Saturday, according to the spokesman for Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces, Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili.
He added that initial estimates indicate that the operations killed at least 700 Houthi rebels.
Meanwhile, al-Maliki said the Houthis’ “ties to external agendas” have brought “chaos and devastation to Yemen”, adding that “what the Houthis are facing in Taiz … drive them to seek illusory victories”.
Early on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said its armed forces carried out 97 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.
The fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces has intensified since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July, displacing hundreds of thousands of people since then.
In mid-September, the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital route for global oil shipments, before anti-Houthi forces stabilised front lines.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, forcing the Yemeni government to retreat to Aden.

articles.summary: Trump-linked drone firm’s Pakistan deal raises questions over US arms thaw  The Times of IndiaDrones, Dollars, And Diplomatic Rifts: Trump-Backed Defence Venture Raises Eyebrows In New Delhi | Opinion News  News18Powerus: The Ambitious American Defence Contractor Fuelling South Asia’s Drone Race  India NarrativePakistan Army’s Drone MoU With US Firm Powerus Triggers Concerns Over Ukraine Drone Tech Transfer and Terror Links  defence.inTrump sons’ company t...
articles.full_text:
TOI correspondent from Washington: An obscure American defence start-up has suddenly acquired an outsized geopolitical significance after signing a memorandum of understanding with the Pakistan army and securing an initial order for unmanned aerial systems, raising questions in Indian strategic circles over whether the deal could be an indicator of a wider reopening of US military supplies to Pakistan.
Powerus, a Florida-based company barely a year old, signed the agreement during a September visit to Pakistan led by its president and co-founder Brett Velicovich, a former US army special operations intelligence analyst. The company says the initial order is limited, but Velicovich has said its longer-term ambition is to combine American and Pakistani technology and potentially establish manufacturing in Pakistan.
“Powerus has received a limited procurement order from the ministry of defence of Pakistan for unmanned aerial systems and associated support. The order represents an expansion of our international defense business. We have also signed a strategic mou. It sets a framework for potential expanded cooperation in unmanned and autonomous systems, subject to definitive agreements and government approvals,” the company said in a September 17 announcement.
“We are proud to support Pakistan’s Ministry of Defence, and the memorandum gives both sides a strategic framework to build upon.” Velicovich added.
The Pakistan deal is particularly notable because Powerus has access to Ukrainian defence technology developed during the war with Russia. In March, it established Powerus USA, in partnership with Wyoming-based G1 Exploration, to commercialise Ukrainian autonomous defence systems. Powerus owns 51% of the venture, while G1 contributed intellectual property covering seven fully developed products and other systems under development.aThe partnership produced the Guardian family of counter-drone interceptors, designed to destroy hostile unmanned aircraft. Powerus says Guardian has been developed with Ukrainian technology and battlefield experience, which have received rave notices in the US. This creates an unusual – and in Indian eyes an unprecedented – chain: Ukrainian drone technology, brought into a US defence company, is now potentially being transferred to Pakistan, a country whose military has been rapidly expanding its own drone capabilities.
The political sensitivity is heightened by Powerus's links to the Trump family. Powerus completed its merger with Nasdaq-listed Aureus Greenway Holdings on October 1 and now trades as Powerus Corporation under the symbol PUSA. Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump are reported to be investors in Aureus through American Ventures; regulatory filings have indicated an indirect stake of about 9.9% in the combined company.
Ironically, the deal has also caused unease in some Pakistani circles because of Powerus’ Israeli links, with one of its co-founders reported to be former IDF officer Ziv Marom. Some analysts are questioning why Pakistan, which already builds its own drones and buys others from China and Turkiye, a company that was founded only last year and sells drones to India too. Others view it as Pakistan -- which is heavily dependent on China for major weapons imports -- diversifying its suppliers.
Indeed, the most intriguing aspect of the Pakistan deal is that Powerus had already entered the Indian defence market. In June, Powerus subsidiary Tandem Defense was reported to have granted Mumbai-based Paras Defence and Space Technologies exclusive licence to manufacture and commercialise the Guardian-1 counter-drone interceptor in India. So effectively, the same American company is now pursuing defence cooperation with both India and Pakistan, which fought a short war in May 2025 in which drones played a prominent role.
The juxtaposition is attracting close attention in military circles in India, which has invested heavily in its strategic relationship with Washington and is viewing the transfer of advanced unmanned technology to Pakistan with concern. Of course, the US has a long history of supplying arms to rival states, and the Powerus arrangements do not by themselves demonstrate a change in policy towards India.
The larger question though is whether Powerus represents something more consequential: a gradual restoration of the US-Pakistan defence relationship -- which has largely been in ice over the past two decades -- in a capital where institutional and congressional oversight is perceived to have broken down with opportunists having a free run.
The Trump administration itself began loosening controls last December when it approved a $686 million package to modernise Pakistan's existing F-16 fleet. The consignment included 92 Link-16 tactical data systems, cryptographic equipment, avionics, training and logistical support. The stated US rationale was “to preserve Pakistan's interoperability with US and partner forces and support counterterrorism and future contingencies.”
Powerus could empower the Pakistani military even more. Drones, counter-drone systems, communications, surveillance and electronic warfare are less politically conspicuous than supplying Pakistan with new fighter aircraft or major offensive weapons, but they are also the technologies whose importance has been demonstrated by the wars in Ukraine and the India-Pakistan conflict.

articles.title: “I am under arrest”: A banyan tree in Pakistan has been chained and ‘arrested’ since 1898 because… - The Times of India
articles.summary: “I am under arrest”: A banyan tree in Pakistan has been chained and ‘arrested’ since 1898 because…  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Seeing criminals in chains is a normal sight, but can you imagine a tree heavily chained? Yes, there is a banyan tree in Landi Kotal, a historic town at the western end of the Khyber Pass in present-day Pakistan, where it is actually chained. Not only this, the heavy chains hold the tree to the ground, while a board attached to it carries the extraordinary words:
“I am under arrest.”
But behind the unique sight is an age-old story that has survived for more than a century, which is part local history and part colonial-era anecdote.
What’s the tale?
As per story, the incident took place in 1898. The area was under British rule in India and that time the officer named James Squid, reportedly intoxicated, said that the tree was moving towards him. He allegedly ordered a mess sergeant to arrest it and have it chained so that it could not escape.
The story has been in Pakistani and international media for years
A report citing former Khyber Rifles mess secretary Captain Nasir Farooq said the officer believed the tree was moving and that it might even “run away” towards Peshawar. The plaque on the tree similarly recounts the tale of an intoxicated British officer ordering the tree to be arrested.
Where is Landi Kotal?
Chained tree at Landi Kotal (Instagram)
It’s the time before Pakistan did not exist as an independent country. The region formed part of British India. Landi Kotal occupied an exceptionally strategic position at the western end of the Khyber Pass. The pass was one of the most important routes between the Indian subcontinent and Afghanistan. The National Army Museum describes Landi Kotal as a British post at the western mouth of the Khyber Pass.
The timing of the tree story is particularly striking. The Khyber region had witnessed serious unrest in 1897, when Afridi tribesmen attacked British posts, including Landi Kotal. The British subsequently reinforced their position in the area. By 1899, the Khyber Rifles were stationed at Landi Kotal and other posts in the pass.
For local residents, the story has sometimes been interpreted as a miniature illustration of colonial authority: an official could supposedly point at an immobile tree and declare it under arrest, and the order would be carried out.
The tree could not protest, of course
The tree is still heavily chained 
The tree could not protest or flee. So the chains remained.
At first glance, it looks like a joke: an intoxicated officer thinking the tree is moving. But the joke becomes darker when placed in the context of a heavily militarised frontier. And now the tree has outlived the authority that supposedly imprisoned it.
Today, the chains are perhaps more powerful as a historical curiosity than as evidence of exactly what happened in 1898. The British Empire is gone, the political map of South Asia has changed, and the Khyber Pass has witnessed generations of upheaval.
It feels strange to see the wooden sign “I am under arrest” today.
A tree cannot be arrested. And clearly it cannot run away anywhere or understand an order issued by a drunken officer. Yet, more than a century later, it still stands in chains often reminding the world of a period when the whole world was ‘chained’ by one power.

articles.summary: US President Trump threatens tariffs of up to 300% as Korea faces pressure over investment  Asia News NetworkTrump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more'  CNBCTrump Says South Korea Deal Includes $8.4 Billion U.S. Oil Project  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comKorea protests US' unilateral announcement on Alaska LNG project  The Korea TimesHow Japan and South Korea Plan to Invest $900 Billion in US  Blo...
articles.full_text:
SEOUL – US President Donald Trump said foreign companies that fail to build factories in the United States could face tariffs of up to 300 percent, as South Korea faces separate pressure from Washington over how it will carry out its $350 billion US investment commitment.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio, on Saturday, Trump presented tariffs and foreign investment as part of his economic record while campaigning for Republican candidates ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Ohio is home to a closely watched Senate race, with the economy and cost of living among major campaign issues.
Trump said overseas companies would be given about a year and a half to build plants in the US before facing tariffs ranging from 150 percent to 300 percent. He also named South Korea alongside China, Japan and Canada while arguing that his tariff policy had pushed foreign companies to invest in US manufacturing.
The remarks came a day after Trump increased pressure on Seoul over the Alaska liquefied natural gas project, which has emerged as a point of disagreement in implementing the two countries’ trade and investment agreement.
South Korea agreed last year to invest $350 billion in the US in return for lowering tariffs on Korean goods from 25 percent to 15 percent. The package comprises $150 billion for shipbuilding cooperation and $200 billion for strategic investment.
Trump this week presented Korean participation in Alaska LNG as part of the strategic investment package. Seoul says otherwise, maintaining that it has agreed only to begin reviewing the project and has not made a final decision on whether or how much to invest.
Trump on Friday rejected suggestions that he had moved too quickly in announcing Korean participation. “I didn’t jump the gun. I mean, they were there and they were represented,” Trump said. He later added that if South Korea did not want to proceed, “that’s okay with me. I’ll just charge them more.”
Seoul’s caution is tied in large part to the project’s economics. Lead developer Glenfarne Group estimates Alaska LNG would cost between $44.5 billion and $54.5 billion. Reuters reported that its cost per unit of annual production capacity would be more than twice that of many recent US Gulf Coast LNG projects.
The project would require an 800-mile, or 1,287-kilometer, pipeline from Alaska’s North Slope to Nikiski, as well as a gas treatment plant and liquefaction terminal.
President Lee Jae Myung said in September that commercial viability had become a sticking point in negotiations with Washington, including how returns would be shared and how losses from unprofitable projects would be handled.
Seoul had pushed to include the term “commercially reasonable” in the investment agreement, Lee said.
Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan has also said Korea should not put money into projects that fail to meet commercial standards, while acknowledging that pulling out of projects under the agreement could expose Seoul to renewed US tariff pressure.
The first confirmed project under the strategic investment package is a gas-fired power plant in Encinal, Texas. South Korea and the US have also discussed building eight large nuclear reactors, but Korean officials say those projects still require separate reviews before any final investment decisions are made.

articles.title: Youth Unemployment in India: Why Growth Must Create Better Jobs - Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.summary: Youth Unemployment in India: Why Growth Must Create Better Jobs  Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.full_text:
Digital Desk
India’s youth unemployment is improving, but educated workers still face job-quality and skills-mismatch challenges. Why better jobs matter for growth.
India’s demographic advantage will mean little if education does not translate into stable, productive and fairly paid employment
India’s growth story is often measured through GDP, infrastructure, investment and the expansion of new industries. But for millions of young Indians, economic progress is ultimately experienced through a much simpler question: Can I find a job that matches my education, skills and expectations?
That is where the employment conversation becomes more complicated.
India’s official data shows that the overall unemployment rate has improved. According to the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) Annual Report 2025, unemployment among people aged 15 years and above was 3.1% in 2025, while youth unemployment among those aged 15-29 stood at 9.9%, down from 10.3% in 2024. At the same time, unemployment among people with secondary education or above was 6.5% in 2025.
These numbers matter. But they do not tell the entire story.
A job is not always a good job
A young person who spends years earning a degree may technically be employed after graduation. But what happens if the job pays too little to cover basic urban expenses? What if a graduate is working far below their qualification level? What if employment is temporary, irregular or offers little possibility of skill development?
That is the problem of underemployment.
The distinction between being unemployed and being inadequately employed is critical. A person working a few hours, accepting work unrelated to their training or remaining trapped in low-productivity employment may not appear in headline unemployment figures in the same way as someone actively searching for a job.
This is why employment policy cannot focus only on reducing the unemployment rate. The quality, productivity, stability and earning potential of jobs matter just as much.
The educated youth paradox
India has expanded access to education dramatically. The PLFS 2025 report says 67.8% of people aged 15 years and above had at least secondary education, while the share was 79.7% in urban areas. Yet unemployment among educated people remains considerably higher than the overall unemployment rate.
The India Employment Report 2024, prepared by the Institute for Human Development with the International Labour Organization, highlighted this paradox: educated young people have higher unemployment rates, reflecting a mismatch between their aspirations and the jobs available. It also identified job creation, employment quality, skills and labour-market inequalities as important areas requiring attention.
This does not mean education has failed.
Rather, it means education and employment have not always evolved at the same speed.
A degree can improve a person's opportunities, but a degree alone cannot create enough productive jobs. When large numbers of graduates compete for a limited pool of suitable positions, qualifications can become an entry ticket rather than a guarantee of meaningful employment.
The skills mismatch cannot be ignored
Employers frequently need practical, technical and digital skills, while many young people enter the labour market with qualifications that do not directly correspond to those requirements.
The World Bank noted in February 2026 that India faces a persistent skills mismatch between what young people are trained for and what firms need. It said India's youth account for roughly 72% of the unemployed and highlighted concerns about the effectiveness of existing skills-training infrastructure.
The answer, however, cannot simply be to tell every young person to acquire another certificate.
India needs stronger connections between education, vocational training, apprenticeships, industry and actual employment opportunities. Skills programmes should be judged not only by how many certificates they issue, but by what happens to trainees afterwards.
Do they get jobs?
Do their earnings rise?
Do they remain employed?
Do they acquire skills that remain valuable as technology changes?
Those are more meaningful measures of success.
The danger of normalising low-quality work
India's large workforce and expanding services economy have created millions of opportunities. Gig work, delivery services, retail, platform-based employment and informal work can provide income, especially when conventional employment is difficult to find.
But flexibility should not automatically be confused with security.
If a highly educated young person is repeatedly forced to accept work unrelated to their qualifications simply to remain financially afloat, the issue is not individual failure. It is also a labour-market question.
Likewise, entrepreneurship should be encouraged, but it cannot become a convenient substitute for creating sufficient salaried and productive employment.
A healthy economy needs entrepreneurs, skilled professionals, technicians, manufacturers, researchers, teachers, healthcare workers and millions of other workers. There is no single employment model capable of absorbing an entire generation.
India's demographic dividend has a deadline
India's young population is frequently described as a demographic dividend. But demographics by themselves do not create prosperity.
A large working-age population becomes an economic advantage only when people can participate productively in the economy.
The PLFS 2025 report estimates that 25% of people aged 15-29 were not in employment, education or training. For those aged 15-24, the corresponding figure was 21%.
These figures should prompt a broader question: What happens to young people between finishing education and finding a meaningful place in the labour market?
Every year spent disconnected from employment can mean lost income, lost experience and delayed financial independence.
For young women, the challenge can be even more complicated because labour-force participation is affected not only by job availability but also by care responsibilities, mobility and social expectations. PLFS data itself shows significant differences between male and female participation in the workforce.
Growth must be felt in the labour market
India does not need to choose between economic growth and better employment. The two should reinforce each other.
Investment in manufacturing can create jobs, but local skills must match those industries. Technology can increase productivity, but workers need opportunities to acquire new capabilities. Infrastructure can connect cities and markets, but smaller towns also need productive employment ecosystems.
The policy conversation therefore needs to move from “How many jobs were created?” to a more demanding set of questions:
What kind of jobs were created?
How much do they pay?
Are they stable?
Do they use workers' skills?
Can workers progress from entry-level employment to better careers?
And perhaps most importantly: Can a young person build an independent life through that work?
The real test of India's growth story
India's growth story should not be judged only by the size of the economy. It should also be judged by whether a graduate can find meaningful work, whether a young worker can improve their income over time, and whether families can see education translating into greater economic security.
Reducing unemployment is important. But reducing underemployment, skills mismatch and low-quality employment is equally important.
For India's young population, economic growth is not an abstract statistic. It is the difference between staying dependent and becoming financially independent, between repeatedly preparing for an opportunity and actually receiving one, and between holding a qualification and building a career.
India's demographic dividend will not be secured by young people simply having jobs. It will depend on whether those jobs allow them to build productive, secure and dignified lives.
That is the employment challenge that deserves as much attention as the growth numbers themselves.

articles.summary: PAN-IIT Amaravati Council will galvanise AP's growth, says CM Naidu  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
VIJAYAWADA: Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu has sought the cooperation of IIT professionals to develop Andhra Pradesh as a global knowledge hub. He expressed confidence that the collective efforts of IIT alumni, educational institutions, industry and the government would contribute to the State’s technological and economic development.
Addressing the media after the PAN IIT Andhra Pradesh Summit 2026 in Vijayawada on Saturday, the Chief Minister said that India’s 23 IITs had produced around five lakh IIT graduates, who had made significant contributions across various sectors worldwide. He said the summit provided a valuable platform for experts from diverse fields to exchange innovative ideas, discuss emerging technologies and explore opportunities for their practical application.
Naidu said the establishment of the Pan-IIT World Council in Amaravati would create one of the world’s largest academic and professional networks. The participation of a large number of IIT alumni from across the country was a reflection of Andhra Pradesh’s growing reputation, he added.
The Chief Minister said the State would leverage the collective knowledge and expertise of five lakh IIT alumni to accelerate development. The summit would facilitate the creation of 100 startup mentors and help Andhra Pradesh emerge as a global knowledge hub. He said the Pan-IIT Council would guide the State in updating academic curricula in line with changing technological requirements and industry needs. The government would also focus on developing entrepreneurial skills among students from the high school level, with the support of the council.
Quantum technology companies had indicated that commercial quantum computers could be manufactured within the next two years, he said. The Chief Minister also noted that mini quantum test labs, including Q-Shiva systems, were being made available even before the proposed 156-qubit quantum system became operational in Amaravati.
He said the upcoming quantum computer being jointly developed by IBM-TCS and L&T would soon begin operations from Amaravati, further strengthening the State’s position in advanced technology.
The Chief Minister said the State aimed to manufacture and eventually export quantum computing equipment, creating various opportunities.
He said the Pan-IIT Council would provide recommendations for the State’s Deep Tech Policy and support the development of advanced technologies, including quantum computing, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, space and defence, healthcare, agritech and water-related technologies. The Chief Minister said the government had undertaken several initiatives with the vision of transforming Rayalaseema into a prosperous region. The Global Horticulture Hub project was launched with the objective of changing the region’s economic and agricultural landscape.
He said Reliance Industries has also come forward to support the establishment and operation of the Indian School of Agriculture.
During the summit, Pan IIT Amaravati Summit 2026 Declaration was released under Naidu’s leadership. The Andhra Pradesh Government and Pan IIT alumni representatives signed the Pan IIT Amaravati Declaration. The declaration announces the establishment of a permanent Pan-IIT Amaravati Council in partnership with the Andhra Pradesh Government and Pan IIT Alumni India.
Pan-IIT Amaravati Venture Fund with Rs 500 crore will be established to promote DeepTech startups, innovation and investments. The Council coordinates with educational institutions, industries and startups across Andhra Pradesh will strengthen the State’s innovation ecosystem. A decision was taken to establish 10 Industry Chairs in universities and educational institutions in partnership with industries to strengthen research and skill development. A network of 100 global IIT mentors will guide startups and aspiring entrepreneurs in Andhra Pradesh.
The declaration also envisages strengthening the startup ecosystem, promoting DeepTech research and establishing Amaravati as a major centre for technology transfer and innovation.

articles.title: Pakistan’s external finances rely on IMF loans and foreign deposits: Report - Social News XYZ
articles.summary: Pakistan’s external finances rely on IMF loans and foreign deposits: Report  Social News XYZ
articles.full_text:
New Delhi, Oct 2 (SocialNews.XYZ) Pakistan’s external financial position remains heavily dependent on IMF lending and deposits from friendly countries, a combination that helped avert repeated balance-of-payments crises but has failed to deliver long-term economic stability, according to a report.
According to a report by Dawn, successive governments have relied on foreign support tied to Pakistan’s geopolitical importance while failing to build a sustainable export-led growth model.
As a result, periods of economic expansion have largely been driven by imports and consumption, leading to recurring shortages of foreign exchange reserves, it added.
A former military ruler benefited from substantial inflows following the September 11 attacks, including aid, debt relief, foreign investment and portfolio flows.
However, the report said that the opportunity to strengthen Pakistan’s export base was largely missed as inflows fueled consumption, imports and real estate activity.
The country later faced a record current account deficit in 2008, triggering a major economic crisis.
Subsequent governments also struggled to break the pattern.
While the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) helped address energy shortages and improve infrastructure, it did not produce the export growth needed to reduce external vulnerabilities. Rising imports once again pushed the current account deficit higher by 2018.
Although later administrations reduced the deficit temporarily, imports surged again following pandemic-era stimulus measures, while global commodity price shocks and political uncertainty added to economic pressures.
Pakistan’s reserve position is increasingly supported by IMF programmes and deposits from countries such as Saudi Arabia and China, according to the report.
However, these funds do not directly generate economic activity or export earnings and remain vulnerable to changing political and financial conditions.
Pakistan has moved from receiving development-oriented assistance and investment flows to depending on costly loans and short-term deposits, the report said warning that without meaningful export growth, economic stabilisation efforts risk turning into prolonged stagnation, leaving the country caught between slow growth and the threat of another foreign exchange crisis.
Source: IANS

articles.title: India’s Rise in Modi era creates opportunities for Chhattisgarh - The New Indian Express
articles.summary: India’s Rise in Modi era creates opportunities for Chhattisgarh  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
Since 2014, under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, India has embarked on a remarkable journey of transformation. Over the past 12 years, the country has expanded its economic and technological capabilities while reshaping its aspirations at home and its standing abroad. From financial inclusion and digital infrastructure to entrepreneurship, manufacturing and space exploration, the Modi era has been marked by an India increasingly confident about its ability to set ambitious goals and build the capabilities to achieve them.
The most consequential change is visible beyond statistics—in the aspirations of India’s people. Young Indians are looking beyond conventional employment towards entrepreneurship and innovation. Women, particularly in rural areas, are moving from being beneficiaries of welfare programmes to becoming earners and entrepreneurs.
Indian enterprises are expanding globally. India’s G20 Presidency in 2023, the inclusion of the African Union in the G20 and initiatives around renewable energy, disaster resilience and the Global South demonstrated a country seeking to contribute solutions to global challenges. Chandrayaan-3’s historic lunar landing provided another powerful symbol of this confidence.
This transformation has been reinforced by the Modi government’s focus on manufacturing and investment. Make in India, followed by Production Linked Incentive schemes, the semiconductor programme and infrastructure expansion, has sought to position India as a competitive global production and tech hub. Investments involving companies such as Micron, Tata Electronics, CG Power, Kaynes Semicon and the HCL-Foxconn joint venture reflect the growing semiconductor ecosystem.
When Startup India was launched in 2016, India had around 500 DPIIT-recognised startups. By March 2026, the number had crossed 2.23 lakh. More than half have emerged from Tier II and Tier III cities.
For Chhattisgarh, this is an opportunity to ensure that our youth need not leave the state to pursue their ambitions. A young entrepreneur in Raipur, Bilaspur, Durg, Bastar or Surguja should be able to build a company from home and take it to national and global markets. Our agriculture, forest produce, minerals, tribal heritage, tourism and emerging opportunities in drones, AI, clean energy and digital services provide a distinctive foundation.
Chhattisgarh is already attracting significant investment. The state’s new industrial policy is built around three pillars—attractive financial incentives, ease of doing business through transparent processes, and fast-track approvals through a single-window clearance system.
The state received investment proposals worth more than `8 lakh crore from 84 companies. Through our New Industrial Policy 2024–30, we are seeking to create an investor-friendly environment. Through Chhattisgarh Investor Connect, we have taken our proposition to Tokyo, Osaka and Seoul. Raipur has also hosted international platforms, such as the Green Steel and Mining Summit and the Chhattisgarh International Trade Expo.
Across Chhattisgarh, more than 26 lakh houses under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana have provided families with greater security and dignity. Nearly complete electrification of railways is strengthening connectivity and opening new possibilities for the economy.
Chhattisgarh’s farmers are central to this transformation. Paddy procurement at Rs 3,100 per quintal, with a ceiling of 21 quintals per acre, has strengthened the state’s agricultural support system. At the national level, PM-KISAN provides eligible farmers `6,000 annually through direct transfers. The next phase of Chhattisgarh’s agricultural development must build on this foundation through diversification, dairy, horticulture, millets and other allied activities.
For Chhattisgarh, the empowerment of women and tribal communities is not a peripheral objective. It is central to our development model.
The same is true of health and education. Ayushman Bharat has expanded access to healthcare. PM-SHRI schools and Eklavya Model Residential Schools are creating new opportunities for children across Chhattisgarh.
Nowhere is our larger vision more important than in Bastar. We want its narrative to encompass culture, tourism, tribal entrepreneurship, investment and opportunity alongside its challenges. Bastar Pandum and our international investment outreach are part of this effort to make Bastar’s rich identity an economic asset without compromising its culture.
The Modi era has created platforms—from Make in India and Startup India to Digital India, Skill India, Nari Shakti and Drone Didi. The next task is to turn these platforms into deeper outcomes. For Chhattisgarh, that means ensuring that a young person can build a company for the world, a woman can become a technology entrepreneur and a tribal producer can capture greater value from local resources.
India’s rise is creating a new horizon of possibilities. Chhattisgarh is determined not merely to witness that rise, but to be an active participant in shaping it.
Vishnu Deo Sai
Chief Minister of Chhattisgarh

articles.summary: Huge fireball erupts as Russian drone hits Kyiv bridge in daylight- video  The Times of IndiaRussia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support  The GuardianRussia strikes another major bridge in Kyiv as attacks on Ukrainian capital escalate  CNNRussian attacks kill six in Ukraine, damage Kyiv's Northern Bridge  The HinduRussia Turns to Striking Kyiv’s Bridges, Threatening a Vital Lifeline  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
A Russian drone struck Kyiv’s Northern Bridge on Sunday, with video showing a huge fireball erupting on the key Dnipro crossing as vehicles continued to travel across it.
Two people were injured in the strike, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, CNN reported.
The strike came as German chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv amid air raid sirens, explosions and the activation of air defence systems. Merz travelled to the Ukrainian capital alongside German economic affairs and energy minister Katarina Reiche to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy amid Russia’s escalating attacks on the city.
“Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks,” Merz said, warning that if Russia is not stopped, its war machine could eventually turn against Europe.
Video footage showed the moment the Northern Bridge was hit, sending a huge plume of fire and black smoke into the sky while cars were still moving across the bridge.
It was the second time the Northern Bridge had been hit in as many days. Earlier, Kyiv’s Southern Bridge, which carries road traffic and the city’s subway system, was struck five times in less than 24 hours.
Ukrainian officials have warned that repeated attacks on bridges could disrupt vital transport links across the Dnipro River and effectively divide the capital. 
Kyiv is split by the river, with government institutions and businesses largely on the right bank and predominantly residential areas on the left bank.
Ukraine’s infrastructure minister said Sunday that Kyiv plans to build several alternative crossings over the Dnipro if attacks on the bridges continue.
The latest Russian threat came after Zelenskyy said Ukraine would step up attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Bangladesh’s post-LDC rules of origin test - The New Nation
articles.summary: Bangladesh’s post-LDC rules of origin test  The New Nation
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh’s LDC graduation is often framed in terms of tariffs, export competitiveness, and the loss of duty-free access. Yet rules of origin may be equally consequential.
They determine whether Bangladeshi products qualify for preferential tariffs based on sourcing, transformation, and value addition.
In the post-LDC era, success will depend not only on export competitiveness but also on whether production processes and sourcing patterns meet increasingly stringent origin requirements.
Rules of origin matter because preferential tariffs depend on proving a product’s origin. They distinguish genuine transformation from simple processing or transshipment.
The WTO recognizes approaches such as changes in tariff classification, specified manufacturing operations, and minimum domestic or regional value addition.
Transparent, predictable, and relatively simple rules are essential because complex requirements can discourage firms from using preferences. Understanding these rules is increasingly important for maintaining market access.
The challenge is particularly significant because its export success has been built on global value chains.
The ready-made garment industry imports substantial quantities of cotton, yarn, fabric, dyes, accessories, and other inputs.
This sourcing model has helped Bangladesh become internationally competitive by enabling firms to combine imported intermediate goods with domestic labor, manufacturing capabilities, and export infrastructure.
However, what is commercially efficient under LDC preferences may not meet stricter post-LDC origin requirements.
The EU underscores the importance of rules of origin. Under its Generalized System of Preferences (GSP) framework, origin requirements apply to both the Everything but Arms (EBA) and the GSP+ arrangements.
Regional cumulation can allow inputs from Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka to count toward origin, subject to specified conditions.
Strategically, preferential access increasingly depends not only on final assembly but also on where intermediate production occurs and the extent of qualifying transformation.
This could reshape Bangladesh’s sourcing decisions. Consider an apparel exporter that imports fabric, cuts and sews garments, and exports them to Europe.
If the applicable post-LDC regime requires more extensive transformation, that sourcing configuration may no longer qualify for the same preference.
The issue is therefore not simply whether the factories can produce garments; it is whether the entire production chain generates sufficient qualifying origin.
The implications extend beyond apparel. Leather goods, footwear, light engineering, plastics, electronics, and other emerging export sectors will also face origin requirements in multiple markets.
A product assembled in Bangladesh from mostly foreign components may contribute to exports and employment while generating relatively little qualifying domestic value.
Conversely, developing domestic suppliers for materials, components, processing, design, testing, packaging, and related services can strengthen both competitiveness and eligibility for origin.
This positions local value addition as a trade policy instrument, not merely an industrial policy objective.
Bangladesh has traditionally pursued export diversification by identifying sectors with market potential. In the post-LDC environment, it will also need to ask a second question: Can these sectors build sufficiently deep domestic or regionally qualifying supply chains to meet future rules of origin? The answer could influence which industries receive infrastructure, skills, finance, technology, and investment support.
Regional cumulation may become particularly important. If future preferential arrangements allow inputs from specified neighboring countries to count toward origin, Bangladesh could integrate more deeply into South Asian production networks.
Such arrangements could enable Bangladeshi firms to source competitively while meeting preferential-origin requirements.
However, this requires effective customs cooperation, reliable certification, traceability, and commercially viable regional supply chains.
Rules of origin also have a significant administrative dimension.
Firms must maintain accurate records of input origins, and customs authorities need effective verification systems. Exporters require expertise in tariff classification, supplier declarations, and origin calculations.
As the EU moves toward more digital origin procedures, Bangladesh must strengthen its systems.
Origin management should therefore become a core export capability, integrated into production and supply-chain decisions rather than treated as post-production paperwork.
The broader economic stakes are substantial. WTO modeling estimates that LDC graduation could reduce exports from graduating LDCs, with clothing particularly exposed, though the magnitude varies by preference utilization, export structure, and destination markets.
For Bangladesh, therefore, preserving market access will require more than negotiating favorable tariffs. It will also require ensuring that Bangladeshi products remain eligible for those tariffs.
The policy agenda should shift from “export promotion” to “origin-ready export development.” The government should map the rules-of-origin market by market, identify the products and supply chains most exposed to stricter requirements, support backward linkages where economically justified, expand regional cumulation opportunities, strengthen customs and certification systems, and provide firms with origin-compliance tools.
Investment incentives should increasingly account not only for export volume but also for domestic and regional value-chain development.
Ultimately, the post-LDC trade battle will extend beyond tariff negotiations to encompass factories, supplier networks, customs systems, and production chains.
Bangladesh’s preferential access will increasingly depend on sourcing inputs, achieving domestic value addition, and demonstrating a qualifying transformation. LDC graduation, therefore, presents both a challenge and an opportunity: reduced preferences can encourage deeper, more sophisticated, and more resilient production capabilities, enabling Bangladesh to pursue higher-value participation in global trade.
(Author: Former Additional Secretary to the Government; Currently, Associate Professor of Public Policy, Bangladesh Institute of Governance and Management–
Affiliated to the University of Dhaka)

articles.title: ‘Re-deployed to their home stations’: US withdraws all bombers from UK’s RAF Fairford after suspected ter - The Times of India
articles.summary: ‘Re-deployed to their home stations’: US withdraws all bombers from UK’s RAF Fairford after suspected ter  The Times of IndiaUS removes all bombers from RAF Fairford base  BBCUS Withdraws All Bomber Planes From UK Airbase Amid Security Concerns  NDTVUK says there are strong indications Iran played a part in a security incident at a US-run air base  AP NewsAll U.S. bombers leave UK air base on concerns of suspected terror plots; more tankers struck near Ira...
articles.full_text:
The United States has withdrawn all its bombers from RAF Fairford in England, a US-run military base that had been used to launch strikes on Iran, following an investigation into a suspected terror plot targeting the facility.
The bombers have been redeployed to their home bases in the United States, a Pentagon official said on Sunday, according to news agency AP.
The official was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on condition of anonymity.
The Pentagon later confirmed the move. “While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon spokesman said in an email, according to Reuters.
B-1 bombers used in Iran strikes
Around a dozen B-1 bombers had been stationed at RAF Fairford, northwest of London.
Aviation watchers, including the Military Air Tracking Alliance, had observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating from the base since the early days of the Iran war.
Observers saw a number of B-1 bombers leave RAF Fairford on Sunday, AP reported.
The bombers had been used for US strikes on Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. 
Britain had allowed the US to use bombers based at Fairford for the operation, according to Reuters.
The withdrawal comes as President Donald Trump weighs options for his war on Iran, including possible new strikes. Trump had initially told Americans that the campaign would last a matter of weeks.
“We have decisions that I’ll make about Iran. Iran’s been decimated. So the only question is — it’ll either be the easy way, or the hard way,” Trump told reporters on Saturday as he left the White House for a rally in Ohio.
Suspected terror plot under investigation
The move from Fairford comes about a week after several people were arrested in connection with suspected plans to carry out terrorist acts at or linked to the base.
A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September.
In total, six people have been taken into custody and subsequently released on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the suspected plot to Tehran. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that Britain had “strong indications” of Iranian involvement.
Iran has denied the allegations, calling claims linking Tehran to the alleged plan baseless. Tehran also summoned the British ambassador over the issue.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that the US aircraft had been removed from RAF Fairford amid security concerns over suspected terror plots targeting the facility.
US maintains military presence in Middle East
RAF Fairford, about 100 miles (160 kilometres) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
The US military continues to maintain a sizeable presence in the region. A US official said on Thursday that the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group were heading towards the Middle East.
The group of ships together carries more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines. The official said the deployment could result in three US aircraft carriers being in the region as early as the end of October.
Trump has said those involved in the suspected plot had planned “big damage”, while US secretary of state Marco Rubio also pointed to the “hands of a foreign actor”.

articles.title: Plague outbreak in Russia? Hundreds quarantined after death of lab researcher - India Today
articles.summary: Plague outbreak in Russia? Hundreds quarantined after death of lab researcher  India TodayNearly 200 People Under Observation After Irkutsk Lab Worker Dies From Plague  The Moscow TimesRussian Researcher Dies Of Plague, Hundreds Quarantined, 5 Hospitals Shut  NDTVScoop: White House monitors suspected plague outbreak in Russia  AxiosHas plague returned to Siberia? Panic in Russia after death of lab worker  euronews.com
articles.full_text:
A 28-year-old anti-plague researcher died after developing severe pneumonia, prompting quarantines and contact tracing in Siberia. The case has raised questions over a possible lab exposure even as officials say no wider outbreak has been found.
A 28-year-old researcher at an anti-plague institute in Siberia has died of severe pneumonia, prompting Russian authorities to place nearly 200 people under medical observation and impose precautionary measures. But authorities have not confirmed that plague was involved.
Russia’s public-health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, has reportedly described the illness as pneumonia of unknown cause and said no microorganisms linked to the researcher’s professional work were detected in her body.
The case has nevertheless fuelled questions about what happened inside the laboratory and whether Russian authorities have been fully transparent about it. The researcher, identified in reports as Darya Shipilova, was admitted to hospital on September 29 after developing severe pneumonia. She was placed on a ventilator but died two days later.
According to the Daily Mail, Shipilova had been working at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute and told medical staff that she had accidentally broken a test tube containing live bacteria. She reportedly became ill while on a field expedition in neighbouring Buryatia, close to Russia’s border with Mongolia, before being transferred to Shelekhov Hospital.
HUNDREDS NOW UNDER WATCH
Authorities moved quickly to trace people who may have had contact with the researcher.
Unofficial reports cited by CNN, including those from the independent regional outlet Liudi Baikala, said nearly 200 people were placed under quarantine at the Shelekhov hospital where Shipilova was treated. The Daily Mail reported that three hospitals in the region were also placed under quarantine measures.
Officials have stressed that there is no evidence so far of a wider outbreak.
Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said all identified contacts were under medical supervision and that none had shown symptoms. Their laboratory test results were negative, he said.
An aluminium plant near the laboratory also ordered employees to wear masks as a precaution, while its director urged residents not to be swayed by what he described as rumours and conflicting reports.
The US has taken note of reports about Shipilova’s death. A US official, cited by American news outlet Axios, said on Sunday that reports of a suspected plague case and related quarantines in Russia were being monitored by the White House.
THE PLAGUE QUESTION
The biggest question surrounding the case is whether the illness was actually caused by plague.
Alexei Tsydenov, head of neighbouring Buryatia, said the woman had died “possibly from the plague”. He also said there was no plague outbreak in Buryatia.
Rospotrebnadzor has not confirmed plague.
Gennady Onishchenko, a former head of the agency, told TASS that the infection was “most likely not the plague”, according to CNN. He also said that even if plague were confirmed, colder weather would make transmission less likely.
The conflicting accounts have added to uncertainty over what caused Shipilova’s illness.
It may be noted that the location of the incident is what makes the case particularly sensitive.
The Irkutsk facility is an anti-plague research institute associated with the study and monitoring of dangerous infectious diseases. That has led to questions about the reported broken test tube and whether Shipilova could have been exposed while handling a dangerous pathogen.
Russian epidemiologist Mikhal Favorov questioned the explanation, according to the Daily Mail, arguing that workers at such facilities use protective equipment. He reportedly dismissed the broken-test-tube explanation as unlikely and suggested that the public might never learn the full circumstances surrounding the infection.
Those comments have fuelled claims of a possible cover-up. An anonymous Russian political Telegram channel, Nezygar, also compared the episode with early disputes over the origins of Covid-19.
However, those claims remain unverified.
MOSCOW MOVES TO CONTAIN THE FALLOUT
Russian authorities have responded by bringing senior health officials into the investigation.
Russia’s chief state sanitary doctor, Anna Popova, travelled from Moscow to Siberia to oversee the response. Kobzev said Popova took part in an emergency meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission after officials received information about a suspected case of a “particularly dangerous infectious disease”.
The governor initially avoided naming the suspected disease.
Shelekhov Mayor Maxim Modin also urged residents to rely on official information and avoid spreading rumours, saying it was too early to draw final conclusions.
WHAT PNEUMONIC PLAGUE WOULD MEAN
Pneumonic plague is one of three forms of plague caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium. Unlike bubonic plague, which is usually associated with infected fleas, pneumonic plague affects the lungs and can spread between people through respiratory droplets.
According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, symptoms can include fever, headache, weakness, shortness of breath, chest pain and coughing. In severe cases, patients can cough up bloody or watery mucus.
The World Health Organisation says plague can have a high fatality rate if untreated but can be successfully treated with antibiotics when detected early.

articles.title: Education-to-Job Gap in India: Why Degrees Aren't Enough - Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.summary: Education-to-Job Gap in India: Why Degrees Aren't Enough  Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.full_text:
Digital Desk
India is producing more educated youth, but the transition from degrees to meaningful employment remains difficult. Why the education-job pipeline needs reform.
India is producing more educated young people, but the transition from classrooms to meaningful employment remains one of the country's biggest economic challenges
For years, the formula seemed straightforward: study hard, earn a degree and find a good job.
For millions of Indian families, education remains the most trusted route to a better life. Parents invest years of savings in school fees, college, coaching and professional courses because they believe qualifications will eventually translate into economic independence.
But the promise is becoming more complicated.
India is producing a larger pool of educated young people, yet the journey from degree to decent employment can still involve years of examinations, unpaid internships, temporary work, repeated applications and jobs far removed from what a graduate studied.
The problem is not that degrees have become worthless.
The problem is that the education system and the labour market are not always moving in the same direction.
More education, but not enough suitable opportunities
India's educational expansion is undeniable. According to the PLFS Annual Report 2025, 67.8% of people aged 15 years and above had completed at least secondary education. Yet unemployment among young people aged 15-29 remained 9.9%, while unemployment among people with secondary education or higher was 6.5%.
These figures do not mean that education causes unemployment.
In fact, education generally improves access to better employment opportunities.
But highly educated young people are also more likely to wait for jobs that match their qualifications and aspirations. That can produce a paradox: more education can raise expectations faster than the economy creates suitable jobs.
A graduate does not necessarily want just any job.
They want work that uses their skills, provides reasonable income and offers a path forward.
When those opportunities are scarce, the degree-to-job pipeline becomes longer and more uncertain.
The first job has become a difficult destination
For many young Indians, getting the first meaningful job is harder than getting the degree itself.
A graduate may send dozens of applications before receiving an interview.
Another may clear multiple recruitment stages but wait months for an appointment.
Someone may accept a job unrelated to their qualification simply to start earning.
Others remain in exam-preparation cycles, hoping for a government position that offers greater stability.
Every month spent waiting has an economic cost.
The graduate loses potential earnings.
The family continues paying living expenses.
Work experience is delayed.
And employers may eventually ask why someone with a degree has little practical experience.
It can become a vicious cycle.
The qualification inflation problem
When a degree becomes common, employers can begin expecting more qualifications for jobs that previously required fewer.
A bachelor's degree becomes the minimum.
Then a master's degree becomes an advantage.
Then certificates, internships and technical skills are added to the list.
The result can be qualification inflation: young people acquire more credentials simply to remain competitive, rather than because each additional qualification substantially improves their ability to perform a job.
For families, this can become expensive.
For young people, it can mean postponing employment.
And for the economy, it can mean an enormous amount of human potential sitting outside productive work.
The answer is not to discourage higher education.
It is to make education more closely connected to actual economic demand.
A degree cannot substitute for work experience
One of the most frustrating contradictions in the entry-level labour market is the demand for experience from people applying for their first jobs.
Employers understandably want workers who can contribute quickly.
But young people cannot acquire meaningful professional experience without being given a meaningful opportunity to begin.
This is where apprenticeships, internships and industry-linked education can play an important role.
Students should not have to wait until graduation to discover what the workplace expects.
Universities, colleges and employers need stronger connections so that practical exposure becomes part of education rather than something students desperately search for afterwards.
Skills training must lead somewhere
India has invested heavily in skills development.
But the success of a training programme cannot be measured simply by the number of people enrolled or certificates issued.
The real questions are more demanding:
Did participants find employment?
Did their earnings improve?
Did they remain employed?
Did the training match what employers actually needed?
The World Bank has highlighted India's persistent skills mismatch and the need to strengthen pathways connecting young people with labour-market opportunities.
That connection is crucial.
A young person does not need another certificate merely for the sake of having one.
They need a skill that someone is willing to pay for.
The coaching economy is filling the gap
Where formal education struggles to provide a clear employment pathway, the coaching industry often steps in.
Competitive examinations have created an enormous ecosystem around preparation for government jobs, professional entrance tests and other recruitment processes.
Coaching can provide useful academic support.
But when young people spend years preparing for a limited number of vacancies, it raises a larger question about the opportunity cost.
A 24-year-old who has spent three years preparing for an examination has not necessarily failed.
But they have spent three years outside a conventional career path.
For a wealthy family, that period may be financially manageable.
For a low-income household, supporting an adult child through several years of preparation can be a serious burden.
The education-to-job pipeline therefore intersects directly with household finances.
Employers also have a responsibility
The responsibility cannot be placed entirely on universities or students.
Employers also shape the labour market.
If entry-level positions demand an unrealistic combination of degrees, years of experience and multiple certifications, young workers can struggle to enter the system.
If companies rely excessively on temporary arrangements without creating genuine pathways to stable employment, graduates may remain stuck in a cycle of short-term work.
And if internships are treated primarily as low-cost labour rather than structured learning opportunities, they do little to solve the experience gap.
A functioning employment ecosystem requires employers to invest in training the next generation of workers, not simply searching for candidates who already possess every required skill.
The government job obsession has a reason
It is easy to criticise young people for chasing government jobs.
But the attraction is understandable.
Government employment is associated with stability, predictable career progression and social security.
When private-sector employment is perceived as uncertain, poorly paid or insecure, a stable public-sector position naturally becomes highly desirable.
The deeper question is therefore not why young people want government jobs.
It is why so many feel that a limited number of government vacancies are among the safest routes to a secure future.
A stronger private employment ecosystem, especially outside the biggest metropolitan areas, could broaden the choices available to young workers.
Small cities cannot be left out
India's employment challenge is also geographical.
A young person in Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi or Hyderabad has access to a very different labour market from someone in a smaller city or district headquarters.
This does not mean every graduate needs to migrate to a metro.
If manufacturing, healthcare, technology, financial services, logistics and other productive sectors expand across smaller cities, young people can build careers without facing the full cost of metropolitan living.
That could also reduce pressure on housing and urban infrastructure.
India's education-to-job pipeline will work better when economic opportunity is distributed more widely across geography.
The cost of waiting is rarely counted
One of the biggest blind spots in the education debate is the cost of waiting.
Suppose a student graduates at 21 or 22 and does not find meaningful work for several years.
Those years represent more than an empty line on a résumé.
They are years without regular income.
Years without retirement contributions.
Years without independent savings.
Years in which parents may continue providing financial support.
Years in which the young person may postpone marriage, housing or other major decisions.
This is why employment should be understood not merely as an economic indicator but as a life-stage transition.
The first stable job often marks the beginning of adult financial independence.
When that transition is delayed, the effects spread across the entire household.
The danger of blaming young people
Young Indians are often told that they lack skills, are unwilling to work or expect too much.
Some graduates may indeed need stronger practical skills.
Some may need to broaden their job search.
But placing the entire burden on young people ignores the other side of the equation.
An economy must create opportunities for the skills it encourages people to acquire.
If millions of students are told that education is the route to prosperity, but suitable jobs remain scarce, the problem cannot be solved simply by telling the next generation to “upskill.”
At some point, the demand side of the labour market has to enter the conversation.
The real reform is to connect the dots

articles.title: Canon to Bring Semiconductor Technology and Service Centres to India - urbanacres.in
articles.summary: Canon to Bring Semiconductor Technology and Service Centres to India  urbanacres.in
articles.full_text:
Canon plans to bring lithography technology and dedicated service centres to India as semiconductor manufacturing projects move forward, marking a potential expansion of the equipment and technical-support infrastructure needed for the country’s chip ambitions.
Toshiaki Nomura, President and CEO of Canon India, said the Japanese imaging and optical technology company had discussed its technology with key semiconductor manufacturers whose projects are under development in India. Canon supplies lithography systems used in semiconductor manufacturing.
“India has been actively promoting semiconductor manufacturing through incentive schemes and has approved multiple projects across semiconductor fabrication, assembly, testing, marking and packaging,” Nomura told PTI. “We bring our technologies to help assist the chip manufacturer to produce chips in India. So that’s a great opportunity for us.”
The company’s proposed role would extend beyond supplying equipment. Nomura said Canon could establish dedicated service centres in India once customer projects are confirmed. Semiconductor manufacturing equipment requires continuous technical support, and he said Canon would need to provide 24×7 assistance to chip manufacturers operating the systems.
“Once the project is confirmed, of course we need 24×7 support to the chip manufacturer. In that sense, we will bring our technologies and service centres in India. That’s our plan,” he said.
Canon has already engaged with major semiconductor projects in the country, but Nomura did not identify specific companies or provide a timeline for individual agreements. He said details would be shared when developments were confirmed. The company’s involvement therefore remains at the discussion and planning stage rather than representing a confirmed equipment contract or operational facility.
The planned support infrastructure comes as India attempts to build a domestic semiconductor ecosystem through government-backed incentives and approved investments. Nearly 12 projects have been approved under the India Semiconductor Mission, covering chip fabrication as well as assembly, testing, marking and packaging.
Among the projects identified in the report are Tata Electronics’ semiconductor fabrication plant in Dholera, Gujarat; Micron’s assembly and packaging facility in Sanand; projects involving CG Power-Renesas and Kaynes Semicon in Gujarat; and Tata Electronics’ semiconductor packaging unit in Assam. These facilities are being developed across different parts of the manufacturing chain, creating demand not only for factories but also for specialised machinery, maintenance and technical expertise.
Nomura said Canon was confident in India’s ability to develop the required ecosystem, although he noted that project timelines were the responsibility of individual chip manufacturers. “Governments and related parties are working very hard to build up this ecosystem. In the near future, this ecosystem will be available,” he said.
Canon has been expanding beyond its traditional imaging and printing businesses into semiconductor equipment, medical systems, and surveillance and security solutions. India is among the company’s focused markets globally, with Nomura saying its operations in the country have recorded double-digit growth consistently. The company’s cameras, printers, multifunction devices and production machines continue to form the core of its Indian business.
The next step for Canon will depend on the confirmation and progress of semiconductor projects and the resulting requirement for lithography equipment and round-the-clock technical support in India.
